About: The Prism — Minimum Deviation & Spectrum

Source

Topic
Geometric optics — refraction through a prism
Concept
As the prism rotates, the deviation δ passes through a MINIMUM at symmetric passage; and because n depends on wavelength, white light fans into a spectrum with violet deviated most.
Serves
Snell's law at both faces, minimum deviation formula, Cauchy dispersion, angular dispersion.
Inquiry
Does δ fall steadily, rise steadily, or turn around as the prism rotates?
Misconception targeted
"More rotation ⇒ more deviation" and "all colours bend the same, the prism just spreads them somehow."

Guided Inquiry

Predict: what does δ do as you rotate?

You rotate the prism from one extreme toward the other. The ray goes in, bends at both faces, and leaves deviated by an angle δ. What does δ do as the incidence angle grows?

Sweep and watch the curve build

Press ▶ Play (auto-sweep) or drag the Prism rotation slider yourself. The δ–i plot below records every setting. Look for the dip.

The scene marks the setting where δ bottoms out. Park there, and watch the ray inside the glass while you do.

Verify: symmetric passage

At the minimum, what is true about the ray inside the prism?

Predict: which colour deviates most?

White light is a mixture of wavelengths, and the glass has a different refractive index for each one. Which colour deviates most?

Two lessons, one cause

Rotate → minimum: δ(i) has a dip at symmetric passage — the standard result n = sin((A+δm)/2)/sin(A/2).

Colour → dispersion: Cauchy's relation n(λ)=a+b/λ² makes n fall as λ rises. So violet, with the larger n, deviates more than red. The angular dispersion between them is about 1.5° for a 60° prism.

You now have the full sim: rotate freely, change the apex, toggle white light. Finish to explore.

The Prism

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A narrow ray of light enters one face of a glass prism, bends there, bends again at the second face, and leaves turned away from its original direction by an angle δ. The sim draws the ray above and plots δ against the angle of incidence below.

What you'll learn

  • How Snell's law at the two faces links the angles i, r₁, r₂ and e.
  • How the apex angle A and those angles fix the total turning δ.
  • What δ does when you turn the prism, and what changes when the light is white instead of one colour.
The angles the sim names: incidence i, refraction r₁ and r₂ inside the glass, emergence e, apex A and deviation δ.

What's on screen

  • The ray: one bright line in monochromatic light, with a short dashed normal at the entry face.
  • Original direction: the grey dashed line the ray would follow with no prism.
  • Deviation δ: the teal arc between that dashed line and the ray that leaves.
  • The plot: δ against i. The teal curve builds as you turn the prism, and the amber dot marks the setting you have now.
  • Readouts: the angles r₁, r₂, e and the deviation δ for the current setting.
See itLook at the opening setting: i = 45°, A = 60°, one wavelength. Watch for: the ray bending at both faces with the teal δ arc beyond the prism, and the amber dot on the plot at i = 45°.

Fixed: the prism is one kind of glass in air, with n = 1.513 at 550 nm. Its index changes with wavelength by a rule given in section 06.

03

Two refractions turn the ray by δ = i + e − A

Snell's law applies at each face, with air outside (n = 1) and the glass index n inside. At entry, sin i = n sin r₁. At exit, n sin r₂ = sin e.

The two normals meet the faces at right angles, so the triangle they make with the apex gives r₁ + r₂ = A. Each face turns the ray toward the base: by i − r₁ at entry and by e − r₂ at exit. The two turns add:

δ = (i − r₁) + (e − r₂) = i + e − A
All angles are measured from the normal at the face they belong to. A is the angle between the two faces.
ir₁r₂eδ
45°27.86°32.14°53.62°38.62°

This row is for A = 60° and n = 1.513. Note r₁ + r₂ = 60°. If n sin r₂ would exceed 1, no angle e exists. The ray is then totally reflected at the second face and does not leave.

See itKeep i = 45° and A = 60°, and read the readouts. Watch for: r₁ = 27.86° and r₂ = 32.14°, which add to A, and δ = 38.62°.
See itRaise the apex angle to 70° at i = 45°. Watch for: the ray turned back at the second face, and the e readout showing "— (total internal reflection)".
04

δ falls to a minimum as i grows, then rises

For a fixed apex angle, δ depends on i alone, because r₁, r₂ and e all follow from it. For A = 60°:

i30°45°50°60°70°
δ50.71°38.62°38.34°39.91°43.87°

So δ neither rises steadily nor falls steadily. It drops to a lowest value, the minimum deviation δm, and then climbs again. Here δm = 38.33°, at i = 49.2°. The bottom is flat: δ stays within 0.5° of δm from about i = 44° to 55°.

At small i the ray meets the second face too steeply to leave. For A = 60° that happens below i = 28.9°, so the plot starts there. The sim draws δm as a dashed line on the plot and gives it in the readouts.

See itFill in the whole curve for A = 60°, then stop at i = 70°. Watch for: the teal curve falling to a dip in the middle and rising again, with the amber dot on the rising side at δ = 43.87°.
05

At the minimum the ray inside runs parallel to the base

A ray can be sent back along its path. So if entering at i leaves at e, then entering at e leaves at i, with the same δ. Each δ is therefore reached at two angles of incidence, except at the lowest point, where the two meet: i = e.

Then r₁ = r₂ = A/2. The ray inside meets both faces at equal angles, so it runs parallel to the base. This is symmetric passage. Putting i = (A + δm)/2 and r₁ = A/2 into sin i = n sin r₁ gives

n = sin((A + δm)/2) / sin(A/2)
For A = 60° and δm = 38.33°, this gives n = 1.513.
A30°40°50°60°70°
δm16.11°22.34°29.51°38.33°50.44°

A larger apex angle gives a larger δm. The sim marks symmetric passage when r₁ and r₂ differ by less than 0.4°.

See itSet i = 49.5° with A = 60°. Watch for: a green dashed ray inside the glass, parallel to the base, and the symmetry readout showing YES.
See itChange the apex angle to 40° and refill the curve. Watch for: δm reading 22.34° instead of 38.33°, and the dip of the curve moved left to about i = 31°.
06

Violet has the larger index, so it is turned more

The index of glass depends on wavelength. The sim uses Cauchy's rule, n(λ) = a + b/λ², with a = 1.5 and b = 4 × 10⁻¹⁵ m². A shorter wavelength gives a larger n.

Lightλn
Red700 nm1.508
One wavelength (the sim's default)550 nm1.513
Violet400 nm1.525

Since v = c/n, violet travels slowest in the glass and is turned most at each face. It leaves with the largest δ and red with the smallest. White light spreads out into a fan of colours, from violet to red.

At A = 60° and i = 45°, red gives δ = 38.14° and violet 39.74°, a spread of 1.60°. The spread depends on i: 1.86° at 40° and 1.46° at 50°. It also grows with A: at i = 45°, A = 30° gives 0.55° and A = 50° gives 1.02°.

See itSwitch to white light at i = 45° and A = 60°. Watch for: a fan of colours leaving the prism with violet turned most, and the Dispersion row reading 1.60°.
See itKeep white light and i = 45°, and reduce A to 30°. Watch for: the fan much narrower, and the Dispersion row falling to 0.55°.
07

Where it matters

  • Measuring n. In a spectrometer one measures A and δm, then uses n = sin((A + δm)/2) / sin(A/2). Near the minimum δ hardly changes with i, so a small error in setting i matters little.
  • Spectra. A prism spectrometer separates the lines in the light from a source. The wavelengths of those lines identify the elements in it.
  • A limit on A. Light passes through only if A is below 2 sin⁻¹(1/n). For n = 1.513 that is about 82.7°.
Go deeper: the thin prism

For a small apex angle, the minimum deviation is close to δm ≈ (n − 1)A. The sim's smallest A, 30°, is not thin, and gives 16.11° against 15.40° from this rule.

08

Summary

In one line. This sim shows how a prism turns a ray by an angle δ, and how that angle changes with the angle of incidence and with the colour of the light.

Key points

  • δ = i + e − A, with sin i = n sin r₁, n sin r₂ = sin e and r₁ + r₂ = A.
  • As i grows, δ falls to a minimum δm, then rises. There i = e, r₁ = r₂ = A/2, and the ray inside is parallel to the base.
  • n = sin((A + δm)/2) / sin(A/2) gives the index from A and δm.
  • Shorter wavelengths have larger n, so violet is turned most and white light spreads out.

Common mix-ups

  • "More rotation always means more deviation." δ falls first, reaches a minimum, and only then rises.
  • "Red bends most because its wavelength is longest." The longest wavelength has the smallest n, so red is turned least.
  • "The prism adds the colours." They are already in white light. The glass turns each wavelength by a different amount.

Things to try on your own

  • For A = 50°, check the δm in the readouts with n = 1.513.
  • For A = 40°, find the i with the lowest δ and compare it with (A + δm)/2.
  • At i = 45°, raise A until the ray stops leaving.
